What to do the day you get your store, in order.

Your store arrives working but empty. This is the order to do things in — each step depends on the ones above it, and doing them out of order is what causes the confusing problems.

Sign in at /admin/ on your own domain, with the username and password emailed to you when the store was built. That login is separate from anything else.

The order

  1. Store settings — your business name, store URL, tax rate. Orders cannot be priced correctly until the tax rate is right.
  2. Payments — connect Razorpay. Until this is done nobody can check out.
  3. Shipping — at minimum a flat rate. A store with no shipping method will not let a customer complete an order.
  4. Look and feel — logo, colours, fonts.
  5. Categories, then attributes if you sell variants.
  6. Products. Do one completely, end to end, before doing fifty.
  7. Pages and navigation — home page sections, About, policies, menus.
  8. Place a test order yourself, pay for it, and refund it.
  9. Only then: WhatsApp, campaigns, recovery, AI.

The test order matters

Before you tell anyone the store is open, buy something from it. Use a real payment method and a real address, then refund yourself. It is the only way to find out whether:

  • Payment actually completes and the order appears in the admin.
  • Shipping was calculated and charged.
  • Tax appears correctly on the order.
  • The confirmation email arrives, and reads the way you want.
  • The order can be fulfilled and a shipment booked.

Nearly every "the store is broken" message traces back to a step above being skipped. Twenty minutes here saves a bad first week.

Business details, currency, tax, and the basics every order depends on.

Settings holds the handful of things about your business that everything else reads. Credentials for outside services live in Integrations instead.

General

SettingWhat it does
Brand nameYour store's name. Appears in the header, page titles, emails and invoices.
Site URLYour store's address. Used to build links in emails and messages — if it is wrong, links in order emails point at the wrong place.
Brand logoUpload rather than paste a URL. PNG with a transparent background works best; it is kept as-is rather than converted, so transparency survives.
Default meta descriptionThe fallback description for pages that have none of their own.
Default share image1200 × 630 px. Used when someone shares a link to a page with no image of its own.
robots.txtEdited here rather than over FTP. Leave it alone unless you know why you are changing it.

Tax

A single tax rate, applied to orders and broken out separately on each one. Set this before you take a real order — changing it later does not correct orders already placed, and those are what your accountant will look at.

Per-product HSN codes are set on the product, not here. The rate here is what gets charged; the HSN is what appears on a GST invoice. Both matter, and they are in different places.

Shipping defaults

Flat rateCharged when no other rule produces a price.
Free shipping overOrder value above which shipping is not charged. Leave empty to never give free shipping.
Shipping markup %Added to live courier rates. Use it if you do not want to pass courier prices through at cost.

Zones and per-weight rates are configured under Shipping — these are only the fallbacks.

Cart recovery

Abandon afterMinutes of inactivity before a cart counts as abandoned. Too short and you chase people who are still shopping.
Maximum messagesA hard cap on how many times one cart is chased. Respect it — this is the difference between a nudge and harassment.

Integrations

Everything that needs credentials from an outside service:

IntegrationWhat it gives you
RazorpayTaking payments — UPI, cards, net banking, wallets
ShiprocketLive courier rates, booking shipments, tracking
Email (SMTP)Order confirmations, receipts, marketing email

InstagramDMs and comment replies in the same inbox
Meta Pixel & CAPIConversion tracking and attribution
Google Analytics 4Page views and ecommerce events
AIContent drafting and the shopping concierge
Storage & CDNWhere product images and video are stored and served

Each has a Test button. Use it — it verifies the credentials actually work rather than only that you typed something.

Secrets are write-only. Once saved, a password or key is never shown back to you. Leaving a secret field blank means keep the current value, not "clear it".

Choosing a gateway, prepaid and COD.

Payments run through a gateway on your own account. Money settles directly to your bank — it never passes through us.

Choosing a gateway

Four are supported. Pick whichever you already have an account with:

GatewayHow the customer paysSetting it up
RazorpayA payment window opens over your store. Razorpay guide
CashfreeA payment window opens over your store. Cashfree guide
PhonePeThe customer goes to PhonePe and comes back. PhonePe guide
PayUThe customer goes to PayU and comes back. PayU guide

You are not limited to one. Configure several and the customer chooses at checkout. You can also switch provider later without rebuilding anything — fill in the new one, clear the old one.

A gateway missing a credential is never offered. It cannot be selected and does not appear at checkout, so a half-finished setup can never take a live order and fail on it. If no gateway is fully configured, checkout offers Cash on Delivery only.

Which one should you pick?

Whichever you can get approved fastest, in practice. They all take cards, UPI, net banking and wallets. The differences that actually matter to you are the rate you negotiated, how quickly settlement lands, and whose KYC you have already passed — not anything in the store.

Start KYC on day one, whoever you choose. It is reviewed by people and takes days. It is the single most common reason a launch slips with everything else ready and waiting.

The webhook

This step is not optional, whichever gateway you use. What confirms a payment is the webhook, not the customer arriving back on your site. Someone who pays and closes the tab straight afterwards still gets their order — but only if the webhook is set up. Without it, customers can pay and their orders will sit unpaid.

Each gateway has its own address:

GatewayWebhook URL
Razorpay/webhooks/payment/razorpay/
Cashfree/webhooks/payment/cashfree/
PhonePe/webhooks/payment/phonepe/
PayU/webhooks/payment/payu/

The exact URL is shown on each integration page — copy it from there rather than typing it. Every incoming call is signature-checked against your own secret before it is trusted, and one that does not verify is ignored, so a forged call cannot mark an order paid.

Already registered the old Razorpay URL? /webhooks/razorpay/ still works and forwards to the new address. There is nothing you need to change.

Incoming webhooks are signature-verified against your secret before they are believed, so a forged callback cannot mark an order paid.

Testing it

Press Test on the integration — that checks the credentials are accepted. Then place a real order and pay for it, because only that exercises the webhook. Refund yourself afterwards from the Razorpay dashboard.

What customers can pay with

UPI, cards, net banking and wallets, depending on what you have enabled in Razorpay. That is controlled on their side, not here.

Cash on delivery

COD sits in the same order pipeline as prepaid — the difference is only when money arrives. Two things worth knowing before you switch it on:

  • COD orders have a materially higher return-to-origin rate. Watch the RTO figure in Shipments once you have volume.
  • You pay the courier both ways on an RTO, so a returned COD order costs you money rather than merely earning none.

Recording a payment taken elsewhere

If someone pays by bank transfer or in person, open the order and mark it paid manually. It then behaves exactly like any other paid order — it can be fulfilled, shipped and reported on.

Refunds

Refunds are issued from the Razorpay dashboard, against the payment. Update the order in your store afterwards so your records and Razorpay's agree.

Zones, rates, weights and connecting Shiprocket.

Shipping has two halves: deciding what to charge the customer, and actually despatching the parcel. You can do the first without the second.

The minimum that works

Set a flat rate under Settings → Shipping and you can take orders today. Everything below is refinement.

Flat rateCharged when no other rule produces a price
Free shipping overOrder value above which shipping is free. Leave blank to always charge.
Shipping markup %Added to live courier rates, if you use them

Zones and rates

Under Shipping you can define zones — groups of pincodes — each with its own methods. Typical setups are "local", "same state", "rest of India", each priced differently.

  • Assign pincodes to a zone by range rather than one at a time.
  • Zones have a priority order, which decides the winner when two of them cover the same pincode.
  • Each zone can have several methods — a flat rate and a free-over-amount, say.

Weight-based rates

Rates can be calculated from real weight. That only works if your products carry real weights:

Weight is set per variant, in grams, on the product. A catalog with no weights will quote the same shipping for a keyring and a coffee table, and you absorb the difference on every heavy order.

Connecting Shiprocket

Shiprocket gives you live courier rates and lets you book shipments from the order screen, without keeping a courier portal open in another tab.

Integrations → Shiprocket:

FieldNotes
Account email and PasswordYour Shiprocket login
Pickup pincodeWhere parcels leave from. Used for rate lookups.
Pickup location nameThe nickname registered in Shiprocket — it must match exactly
Channel IDOptional
Auto-create shipment on paidBooks the shipment automatically when an order is paid
Tracking webhook tokenA secret you choose; set the same one on the Shiprocket webhook so tracking updates arrive automatically
Package dimensionsDefault length, breadth and height in cm
Default item weightGrams, used when a variant has no weight of its own

Set the default dimensions to something honest. Couriers charge on volumetric weight as well as actual weight, so a default box far larger than what you really ship quietly inflates every rate you are quoted — and every rate you pass on.

Automatic or manual

With Auto-create shipment on paid on, a shipment is created as soon as an order is paid. Leave it off while you are learning the flow, so you see each step before it happens on its own.

Logo, fonts, colours, header and footer.

Appearance controls how the storefront looks without touching a stylesheet. Every change is saved as a draft first, so you can experiment on a live store without customers seeing half-finished work.

Draft, publish, discard, restore

ActionWhat it does
SaveKeeps your changes as a draft. The live store is unchanged.
PublishMakes the draft live.
DiscardThrows the draft away and goes back to what is published.
RestoreBrings back the previously published version — the undo for a bad publish.

Work in drafts and publish once. The temptation is to publish after each tweak; the result is customers watching your store change under them for an hour.

Starting from a theme

There are 28 themes to start from — 19 light and 9 dark. Each one is a complete look rather than a colour swap: it sets the fonts, the card treatment, the header style, the page width, the spacing and the type scale together.

Applying one fills in every setting on this page. Nothing is locked afterwards — change anything you like and it stays changed. Most stores pick the closest theme, adjust the colours to their brand, and stop.

Applying a theme lands in the draft like any other change, so you can try several and publish none of them.

Light, dark or automatic

SettingWhat visitors see
Always lightThe light version, whatever their phone is set to.
Always darkThe dark version, always.
Match their deviceLight or dark depending on their own setting.

Check your product photography before choosing dark. Images shot on a white background sit in bright rectangles on a dark page and look cut out. Dark suits catalogues shot on dark or transparent backgrounds; it rarely flatters plain white packshots.

Width, spacing and type size

These are the settings that make two stores actually look different. Colour and font alone do not — the proportions do.

SettingOptionsWhat it changes
Page widthNarrow, Default, Wide, Full width How far content spreads. Full width is edge to edge with only a gutter.
SpacingCompact, Normal, Roomy, Airy The vertical gap between sections. Airy reads as premium; compact fits more above the fold.
Type scaleSmall to Extra large Base text size. Everything else is derived from it.
Heading scaleSubtle, Balanced, Dramatic How much bigger each heading is than the last.
Hero layoutCentred, Split, Wide banner How the top of the homepage is arranged.

Your own CSS

For the last few percent there is a custom CSS box. It is applied after everything else, so it can override any of the above.

This is the one part of Appearance that can break your storefront. Everything else is a fixed set of choices that cannot produce an invalid page; CSS you write yourself can. Keep it short, and if the store looks wrong after an edit, empty this box first before looking anywhere else.

Logo and colours

Six colours drive the whole theme:

InkBody text and headings
CTAButtons — Add to cart, Checkout
AccentHighlights, badges, links
BackgroundThe page
Header backgroundThe bar at the top
Footer backgroundThe block at the bottom

Check contrast before publishing. A pale CTA on a pale background looks tasteful on your monitor and is invisible on a phone in daylight. The Add to cart button is the one that has to be obvious even when the rest is subtle.

Fonts

Body and heading typefaces are chosen separately, from: Inter, Poppins, Montserrat, Roboto, Work Sans, DM Sans, Nunito Sans, Playfair Display, Lora, Merriweather, Fraunces and Space Grotesk.

A common pairing is a serif for headings (Playfair Display, Lora, Fraunces) with a sans for body (Inter, DM Sans, Work Sans). Using the same face for both is also fine, and safer.

Header styles

StyleBest for
Inline navThe default. Logo left, menu beside it.
Centered logoFashion and lifestyle, where the brand leads.
Search firstLarge catalogs, where people arrive knowing what they want.
MinimalMenu tucked into a drawer. Very few products, or a strong visual home page.

The header can be sticky or static, and you can add an announcement bar above it for a sale or a shipping cut-off.

Footer

Columns gives you your own link groups; Centered is a minimal single block.

Product cards

ClassicBordered, conventional, easy to scan
MinimalBorderless, image-led
DetailSale badge and a second image on hover

You also choose the image aspect ratio and how densely the grid packs. Pick a ratio and then shoot or crop all your product photos to it — mixed ratios are the single most common reason a catalog page looks amateur.

Corners and buttons

Corner radius and button shape — rounded, sharp or pill — are applied consistently everywhere, so the store looks designed rather than assembled.

Social links

Instagram, Facebook, X and YouTube appear in the footer. Leave one blank and it is simply not shown.

Adding products, variants, images, pricing and stock.

A product is the thing you sell. If it comes in sizes or colours, those are variants of one product — not separate products.

Adding a product

Products → Add product. The fields, and what each actually affects:

FieldWhat it does
NameWhat customers see, and what search matches against.
CategoryWhere it appears in navigation and category pages.
DescriptionThe body copy on the product page.
PriceThe base price. Variants can override it individually.
Statusdraft, active or archived. Only active products appear on the storefront.
HSN codeStored per product, for GST-compliant invoicing.
Meta title / descriptionOverrides for search results. Optional — sensible defaults are used.

Leave it in draft while you work. A product saved as active with no photos and a placeholder price is live to customers the moment you press save.

Variants

Variants are generated from attributes — Size, Colour, and whatever else you define. Define the attribute once, reuse it across products. See Categories and attributes.

Each variant carries its own:

SKUYour own code. Used on picking lists, exports and stock updates.
PriceOverrides the base price for that combination.
Compare-at priceThe struck-through "was" price. Leave blank for no discount display.
Weight in gramsWhat shipping rates are actually calculated from.
ActiveSwitch off a combination you no longer sell without deleting its history.

Fill in the weights. Shipping is calculated from them. A catalog with no weights quotes the same shipping for a keyring and a coffee table, and you pay the difference on every heavy order.

Stock

Per variant, under the same form:

Track stockOff for made-to-order or unlimited items.
On handHow many you have.
Low-stock thresholdWhen it starts appearing in low-stock reports.
Allow backorderWhether customers can buy past zero.

Set the low-stock threshold to cover your restock lead time, not to 1. Finding out at zero is finding out too late.

Images

  • Upload several; drag to reorder; set one as primary — that is the one on category pages and in search.
  • Write alt text on each. It is read aloud to customers using a screen reader, shown when an image fails to load, and read by search engines.
  • Shoot everything to the same aspect ratio. Mixed ratios make a tidy catalog look untidy.
  • Images are compressed to WebP automatically. Upload the good version; do not pre-shrink.

Custom product sections

Extra titled blocks on the product page — care instructions, sizing, materials, what's-in-the-box. Better than one enormous description, because customers scan rather than read.

Loading a catalog from a spreadsheet

Everything above is one product at a time, which is the right way to do your first few and the wrong way to do four hundred. Products → Import takes a spreadsheet instead, and the same tool changes prices or stock in bulk afterwards. It has its own chapter: Importing a catalog.

A sensible workflow

  1. Create the attributes you need once, before the first product.
  2. Do one product completely: photos, description, variants, weights, stock, SEO.
  3. Look at it on the storefront, on a phone.
  4. Fix whatever is wrong — then do the rest, having learned it once.

Loading products from a spreadsheet, and changing prices or stock in bulk.

Typing in four hundred products one at a time is nobody's idea of a launch. Products → Import takes a spreadsheet instead: download the template, fill it in, and upload it as .xlsx or .csv. The same tool updates what is already there, so it is also how you change three hundred prices at once.

The import runs on the server, not in your browser. Start it and close the tab — a large catalog with photos to fetch keeps going without you, and Products → Import shows you where it got to whenever you come back.

You do not have to use our headings

After the upload, a screen shows every column in your sheet with the first few values under it, next to what we think that column is. Correct anything guessed wrong, set your own working columns to Do not import, and press start.

This is what makes an export straight out of Tally, Vyapar, Busy or a marketplace usable without editing it first — you match the columns once on screen instead of renaming them in Excel. Ordinary names are recognised on sight, so MRP, Qty, Barcode, Rate and Title all arrive already filled in.

Nothing is read into your catalog until you press start, and any column you leave unmatched is simply not imported — products that already exist keep whatever they had in that field.

One row per variant

A product sold in three sizes is three rows sharing one Handle. The first row carries the name, description and category; the rest need only their own SKU, options, price and stock. A product with no variants is a single row.

The handle is what ties them together and what makes a second upload safe. Keep it stable — blue-cotton-shirt, or your own item code — and the same sheet uploaded twice updates that product rather than creating a duplicate.

ColumnWhat to put in it
HandleAnything, as long as it is the same on every row of that product and unique to it. Leave it blank and the name is used.
OptionsWhat makes this variant different, as Size: M, Colour: Blue.
SKUMust be unique across the whole store. Leave it blank and one is generated.
Price / Compare at priceIn rupees. On a variant row it is that variant's price. Compare-at is the struck-through figure.
CategoryMen > Shirts. Categories that do not exist are created.
Statusdraft, active or archived. Blank means draft, so nothing goes live by accident.

The four things people use it for

If you want toDo this
Add new productsGive each one a handle nothing else uses.
Change prices or stock in bulkUpload a sheet of just Handle and the columns you are changing. Everything you leave out stays as it is, variants included.
Fix a mistakeCorrect the sheet and upload the same file again. Matching handles update rather than duplicate.
Check before committingTick Check it first on the matching screen. Every row is read and problems are listed, but nothing is written.

Photos

Put web addresses in the Images column, separated by commas, and they are downloaded onto your own store as the import runs. The first one becomes the main photo.

They have to be addresses that anything can open. A link to a file in your Google Drive or a shared folder needs a login, so it arrives as nothing — which is the single most common reason products come in without pictures. Uploading the same sheet again does not fetch them a second time, and photos you added by hand in the admin are never touched.

What you get at the end

The import lists what it did, one line per product rather than per row, each marked New or Updated with its variant and photo counts and a link straight to it. Two things on that list are worth a glance:

  • none under photos usually means an image address that could not be opened.
  • Draft means the product is in your catalog but not on your storefront yet.

Anything that could not be imported is listed separately, with the line number it has in your sheet and what was wrong with it — a status that is not one of the three allowed words, or a SKU already used by a different product. Fix those rows and upload the same file again; the ones that went in the first time are updated, not duplicated.

Try it on five rows before you try it on five hundred. Import a handful, look at them on the storefront, and check the price, the stock figure and the photos are what you expected. A mistake in the sheet is a mistake repeated on every row, and it is far quicker to find it on five products than to correct four hundred afterwards.

Organising the catalog so people can find things.

Categories are how customers browse. Attributes are how a product turns into variants. They are set up separately, and both are worth doing before you add many products.

Categories

Categories nest — a parent with children, for example Clothing → Shirts. Each has its own image and SEO fields, so a category page can rank on its own rather than only funnelling from the home page.

FieldNotes
NameWhat customers see.
ParentLeave blank for a top-level category.
ImageUsed on category tiles on your home page.
Meta title / descriptionFor search results.

Fewer, broader categories beat many narrow ones at the start. A category with two products in it looks like an empty shop. You can always split one later; merging is harder.

Categories are not navigation

Creating a category does not put it in your menu. Menus are built separately, under Navigation — see Pages and navigation. This is deliberate: you often want a category to exist and be linked from a page or a campaign without cluttering the main menu.

Attributes

An attribute is a property with a set of values — Size with S, M, L, XL, or Colour with the colours you stock. Define it once under Attributes and reuse it on every product.

How variants are generated

On a product, pick the attributes that apply and the values you stock. The combinations become variants. Two attributes with three values each give nine variants, each with its own SKU, price, weight and stock.

Only tick values you actually stock. Selecting every colour "to be safe" generates dozens of variants you then have to price, weigh and set to zero stock — and any you forget become buyable.

Naming them well

  • Be consistent: Colour everywhere, not Colour on one product and Color on another. They are different attributes and customers see both.
  • Use the customer's words. Navy, not PMS 289.
  • Keep sizes in a sensible order — S, M, L, XL, not alphabetical.

Do this first

Attributes before products. Adding a variant dimension to a product that already has orders against it is messy; getting it right at the start costs nothing.

Collecting and moderating customer reviews.

Reviews are the cheapest conversion improvement you have, and they are also a moderation responsibility. Nothing appears on the storefront until you approve it.

Approving reviews

New reviews arrive as pending. Under Reviews you approve or reject each one. Approving publishes it on the product page and counts it towards the product's rating.

StatusVisible on the storefront
pendingNo
approvedYes
rejectedNo

Do not reject a review for being critical. A page of nothing but five stars reads as fake and converts worse than a mix. Reject spam, abuse and anything about a competitor — not honest disappointment. A thoughtful reply to a three-star review sells more than its absence.

Keep the queue short

A growing backlog is a real cost: those are customers who took the trouble to write something and cannot see it. Check it on a schedule, not when you remember.

Getting more of them

  • Ask after delivery, not after purchase — they need the product in hand.
  • Ask once. A second reminder annoys more people than it converts.
  • Make it one tap. Every extra step halves the response.
  • An automated journey can do this — see Campaigns and journeys.

How ratings show up

Each product carries an average rating and a review count, shown on the product page and on cards. Only approved reviews count towards it.

Booking couriers, labels, pickups and RTO.

A shipment is a parcel. Booked from the order screen through Shiprocket, so you never have to keep a courier portal open in another tab.

Booking a shipment

  1. Open a paid order and create the shipment.
  2. Pick a courier from the rates offered. They differ on price, speed and how well they serve that pincode.
  3. An AWB — the tracking number — is assigned.
  4. Print the label, and the manifest if your courier wants one.
  5. Schedule the pickup.

With Auto-create shipment on paid switched on, step one happens by itself as soon as an order is paid.

Choosing a courier

The cheapest is not always right. Weigh up the rate against delivery time and, most of all, whether that courier is any good at the destination pincode. A cheap courier that fails delivery costs you the return leg and the customer.

Tracking

Once the tracking webhook is configured, status updates arrive automatically as the parcel moves — no polling, no checking by hand. Each shipment carries its courier name, AWB, current status and a tracking URL you can share.

Parcels that stop moving

A shipment that has not changed status for a few days usually means something went wrong at the courier: a failed delivery attempt nobody logged, a parcel sitting in a hub, an address the driver could not find.

Chase these before the customer does. A proactive message about a delay is a completely different conversation from an apology after a complaint.

RTO — returns to origin

RTO is where COD margin goes to die. You pay the courier both ways, so a returned COD order costs you money rather than merely earning none. Watch the RTO rate as a number, not a feeling.

What actually reduces it:

  • Confirm COD orders before booking — a WhatsApp message asking them to confirm.
  • Check the phone number. Unreachable customer, failed delivery, parcel comes back.
  • Set delivery expectations honestly. People refuse parcels that arrive later than promised.
  • Watch repeat offenders. The same number refusing several COD orders is a pattern.
  • Nudge towards prepaid with a small discount. It is usually cheaper than the RTO rate.

Cancelling a shipment

Cancel it from the order if the order falls through. Do this before the pickup — once the courier has the parcel, it is a return rather than a cancellation.

Package dimensions

Couriers charge on volumetric weight as well as actual weight. Default dimensions are set in the Shiprocket integration; keep them honest. A default box much larger than what you really ship quietly inflates every rate you are quoted, and every rate you pass on to customers.

How every integration works

Keys, the webhook, and going live.

Razorpay takes the money. It is the one integration you cannot launch without.

Before you start

  1. Create an account at razorpay.com.
  2. Complete KYC — PAN, bank account, business proof. This is a review by humans and takes days, not minutes.
  3. Until KYC is approved you can only use Test mode.

Start KYC on day one. It is the single most common reason a launch slips: everything else is ready and the payment account is still under review.

Getting your keys

  1. Razorpay Dashboard → Settings → API Keys.
  2. Generate a key. You get a Key ID and a Key Secret.
  3. The secret is shown once. Copy it before closing the dialog.
  4. Test mode and Live mode have different keys. Note which you are using.

Entering them

Integrations → Razorpay:

FieldValue
Key IDFrom Settings → API Keys. Starts rzp_test_ or rzp_live_.
Key secretThe one shown once when you generated the key.
Webhook secretA secret you invent. You will paste the same value into Razorpay in the next step.

Save, then press Test. It should pass before you go further.

The webhook — do not skip this

The webhook is what marks an order paid. The customer being redirected back after payment proves nothing — they might close the tab, or someone could forge the return. Without the webhook, people will pay and their orders will sit unpaid.

  1. Razorpay Dashboard → Settings → Webhooks → Add New Webhook.
  2. Webhook URL: copy it from the Razorpay card in your store. It ends /webhooks/razorpay/.
  3. Secret: the exact same value you entered as "Webhook secret".
  4. Active events: tick at least payment.captured and payment.failed.
  5. Save.

Incoming webhooks are signature-verified against your secret before they are believed, so a forged callback cannot mark an order paid.

Testing properly

  1. While still in Test mode, place an order using Razorpay's test card numbers.
  2. Check the order appears as paid in your admin. If it stays pending, the webhook is not reaching you.
  3. Switch to Live keys once KYC is approved.
  4. Place one real order with a real card and refund yourself. Test mode does not exercise the same path as live.

Going live

  • Swap Test keys for Live keys in the integration.
  • Add a separate webhook for Live mode in Razorpay — test and live webhooks are configured independently, and forgetting this is a classic launch-day failure.
  • Enable the payment methods you want in Razorpay: UPI, cards, net banking, wallets. That is controlled on their side.

Settlement and refunds

Money settles from Razorpay to your bank on their schedule, typically T+2. Refunds are issued from their dashboard against the payment — then update the order in your store so both records agree.

Creating the Meta app

  1. developers.facebook.com → My Apps → Create App → type Business.
  2. Add the WhatsApp product to it.
  3. Under WhatsApp → API Setup, add and verify your phone number.

Getting a permanent token

The token shown on the API Setup page expires in 24 hours. Use it to test if you like, but if you save it as your access token everything stops working tomorrow with no obvious cause. Create a System User token instead.

  1. business.facebook.com → Business Settings → Users → System Users.
  2. Create a system user with the Admin role.
  3. Add Assets → your app → full control.
  4. Generate New Token → select your app → permissions whatsapp_business_messaging and whatsapp_business_management.
  5. Set expiry to Never. Copy the token — it is shown once.

Entering it

FieldWhere it comes from
Phone number IDMeta → WhatsApp → API Setup. A long number, not the phone number itself.
Access tokenThe permanent System User token from above.
Business Account ID (WABA)Same page. Optional, but needed for templates.
Webhook verify tokenAny secret you invent. You paste the same value into Meta next.
App secretMeta App → Settings → Basic. Verifies inbound messages really come from Meta.

The webhook

  1. Meta App → WhatsApp → Configuration → Webhook → Edit.
  2. Callback URL: copy from the WhatsApp card in your store. It ends /webhooks/whatsapp/.

  4. Verify and save. Meta calls your URL immediately to check it — if this fails, the token does not match or the URL is wrong.
  5. Subscribe to the messages field.

WhatsApp does not let you message someone out of the blue with free text. Anything you initiate must use a template approved by Meta.

Two separate things: the Meta Pixel and Conversions API for Facebook and Instagram ads, and Google Analytics 4 for everything else. Connect them before you spend money on advertising, not after.

Meta Pixel

  1. business.facebook.com → Events Manager.
  2. Connect Data Sources → Web → Meta Pixel, and name it.
  3. Copy the Pixel ID — a long number.
  4. Paste it into Integrations → Meta Pixel & CAPI.

That alone gets you browser-side tracking. It is also the half that ad blockers remove.

Conversions API

This is the half that actually survives. A large share of your visitors block the pixel, use Safari's tracking protection, or are on iOS with tracking off. The Conversions API sends the same events from your server, where none of that applies. Without it, Meta under-reports your sales and optimises your ads against incomplete data.

  1. Events Manager → your dataset → Settings → Conversions API.
  2. Generate access token. Copy it — it is shown once.
  3. Note the Dataset ID on the same page.
FieldWhat to enter
Pixel IDFrom Events Manager.
Dataset IDFor the Conversions API. Often the same as the Pixel ID.
CAPI access tokenThe token you just generated.
Test event codeOptional. Only while testing — see below.

  1. Events Manager → your dataset → Test Events.
  2. Copy the test event code shown there into the integration.
  3. Browse your store and place a test order.
  4. Events should appear in Test Events within seconds.
  5. Clear the test event code afterwards. Events sent with it are not counted as real conversions.

Leaving the test code in place is the classic mistake. Everything looks like it is working, and none of it counts. Clear it once you are satisfied.

Why events are not double-counted

With both halves running, the same purchase is reported twice — once from the browser, once from the server. Each event carries a shared id so Meta collapses the pair into one. You do not need to do anything, but it is worth knowing when a number looks doubled: check the event id before assuming a bug.

Google Analytics 4

  1. analytics.google.com → create a GA4 property if you have none.
  2. Admin → Data Streams → Web, and add your store's URL.
  3. Copy the Measurement ID — it starts G-.
  4. Paste it into Integrations → Google Analytics 4.

Page views and ecommerce events are sent automatically. No tag manager needed.

Checking both work

WhereWhat to look for
Meta Events Manager → Test EventsEvents arriving as you browse
GA4 → Reports → RealtimeYourself, within a minute
Your own ReportsSales by channel — this is the honest one

Your own reports are the tiebreaker. When Meta claims more sales than you made, believe your order table. Ad platforms are optimistic about their own contribution by design.

Both are opt-in: leave the fields blank and no third-party script loads at all. If you operate where consent is required, that is your obligation to handle — and leaving them blank is a legitimate choice.

By default product images live on the store's own disk. Connect object storage and uploads go there instead, served through a CDN — faster for customers, and it stops images filling your server.

When you need this

  • Your catalog is large, or you use video.
  • You are near your disk quota.

A small catalog on local storage is fine. This is not a day-one task.

ProviderNotes

Amazon S3The original. Watch egress charges.

  1. Create the bucket.
  2. Make objects publicly readable — customers' browsers fetch them directly.
  3. Create an API token scoped to that bucket only, with read and write.

If you already have images on local disk, there is a migration that copies them to the bucket and rewrites the URLs. It runs in phases — copy, then rewrite, then clean up — and never deletes anything before verifying it arrived.

  1. Connect the bucket and confirm a new upload lands there.
  2. Start the migration.
  3. Watch the store while it runs. Images stay served throughout.
  4. Only after it reports done are the local copies removed.

Take a backup first anyway. The migration is careful, but a backup costs you five minutes and removes the question entirely.

  1. Press Test.
  2. Upload an image to a product.
  3. Right-click the image on the storefront and check the URL — it should be your CDN or bucket, not your store's domain.
  4. Open that URL in a private window. If it will not load, the bucket is not public.

Ask questions of your store in plain language.

Your store can be connected to Claude or ChatGPT directly, so you can ask questions in plain language and get answers from your real data — "which products are quietly running out of stock?", "what did last month's campaign actually earn?"

This costs nothing per question. It runs on the Claude or ChatGPT subscription you already pay for. No API key is involved and no tokens are billed to your store — unlike the AI provider, which is a separate thing for work that runs unattended.

Before you start

  • A paid Claude or ChatGPT account that supports custom connectors.
  • Your store reachable over https. A plain http address is rejected outright.
  • An admin account with settings permission — you connect as yourself.

Switching it on

  1. In your store admin, open MCP connector under Settings.
  2. Turn the connector on. It is off until you do — nothing starts accepting connections just because the feature exists.
  3. Copy the connector URL shown. It is your store's address followed by /mcp.

If the page warns about http. Connectors require https. Set Site URL under Settings → General to your real https:// address and the warning goes away. This is the most common reason a connection fails before it starts.

Connecting Claude

  1. Claude → Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector.
  2. Paste the URL.
  3. You are sent to your own store to sign in.
  4. Sign in with your admin account and approve the request.

Connecting ChatGPT

  1. ChatGPT → Settings → Connectors → Create.
  2. Paste the same URL, then sign in and approve.

You do not enter a client id or a secret anywhere. Both register themselves, and the sign-in happens on your own store — your credentials are never given to the assistant.

What it can see

Three tiers, and you decide where the line sits.

TierWhat it doesDefault
Read Sales, orders, customers, catalog, stock, shipping, campaigns, SEO. On
Draft Writes suggested copy to the review queue — and nowhere else. You still apply it. On
Write Changes live data: stock, coupon on/off, review moderation, publishing copy. Off

Your staff roles apply

Every tool checks the same permission as the admin screen showing the same data. Connecting as someone who cannot see orders gives an assistant that cannot see orders either. There is nothing extra to grant, and nothing reachable that you could not already open yourself.

Turning writes on

Leave writes off to begin with. Asking questions is where most of the value is, and read-only means the worst case is disclosure of something you can already see. Switch writes on later, deliberately, once you know how you use it. Everything it changes is recorded in your activity log, marked as having come from the connector.

Things worth asking

  • "Which variants are below their low-stock threshold?"
  • "Compare revenue this month against last, and tell me what changed."
  • "Which products get looked at a lot and rarely bought?"
  • "What did people search for that returned nothing?"
  • "Draft descriptions for the products that have none." — lands in the review queue.
  • "Which coupon actually made money, and which one just discounted people who would have bought anyway?"
  • "What does my storefront look like at the moment?"
  • "Show me the dark themes, and draft the closest one to my brand colour." — lands in the appearance draft for you to look at before anything is published.

Changing how the store looks

It can read your current theme, list what is available, and either draft a change or publish one. A drafted change goes to Appearance exactly as if you had made it by hand — you see it, publish it, or discard it. Nothing reaches visitors until you say so.

Publishing directly is possible, and needs writes switched on. If you would rather it never changed the live storefront on its own, ask it to draft rather than publish — or leave writes off entirely, in which case it can only look.

Undoing a theme change made this way is the same as undoing one you made yourself: restore the last published version from Appearance.

The MCP page lists your active connections. Revoke ends one immediately — do that if you stop using an assistant, or if a device is lost. You can only see and revoke your own.

Turning the connector off stops new connections as well as hiding it, so it is a real off switch rather than a cosmetic one.

Why this is safe to do

  • You sign in on your own store, not in the assistant. It never sees your password.
  • Tokens are stored hashed, so a copy of the database does not hand over live access.
  • Read-only by default, with writes behind a separate switch.
  • Your roles are enforced per tool, not just at the door.
  • Revocable at any moment, from the same page.

Most people who put something in a cart do not buy it. Recovery chases those carts on a channel you choose, with wording you can test.

How a cart becomes abandoned

A cart is marked abandoned after a period of inactivity you set under Settings → Cart recovery. Contact details are captured on the cart before payment, which is what makes the cart reachable at all.

Do not set the window too short. Thirty minutes catches people who are still deciding, and a nudge that arrives while someone is mid-thought reads as surveillance. A few hours is usually right.

Message variants

You write several versions of the nudge and the system rotates between them, then reports which actually recovered carts. That is the difference between knowing and guessing.

Each variant has:

ChannelWhatsApp or email
ContentYour copy, or an approved WhatsApp template
ActiveSwitch a variant off without deleting its history

Test one thing at a time

Two variants differing only in the offer tells you whether the discount matters. Two differing in tone, timing and offer tells you nothing.

Send caps

A hard limit on how many times one cart is chased, set in Settings. Respect it. The difference between a helpful nudge and being blocked is roughly two messages.

Writing one that works

  • Be useful, not needy. "Your cart is still here, and the link below rebuilds it" beats "Did you forget something?"
  • Name the product. A generic reminder is easy to ignore.
  • One link, straight back to the cart. The link rebuilds their exact basket.
  • Do not open with a discount. Train people to abandon carts and they will. Save the offer for a second message, if at all.
  • Answer the real objection. Often it is delivery cost or time, not price. Saying "delivered in 3 days, free over ₹X" recovers more than 5% off.

One-click restore

The link in the message rebuilds the exact cart on any device. They do not have to find the products again — which is the step most people will not repeat.

Cart recovery performance in Reports shows sends, carts recovered and revenue recovered, per variant. Judge on revenue recovered, not open rates.

Broadcasts, audiences and automated sequences.

Two different tools. Campaigns are one-off broadcasts you send. Journeys are automated sequences that run themselves when a customer does something.

Campaigns — one-off broadcasts

A WhatsApp broadcast to an audience you define.

  1. Choose an audience. Not everyone — see below.
  2. Write the message, using an approved WhatsApp template.
  3. Preview the audience. You see exactly who it resolves to, and how many, before anything sends.
  4. Schedule or send. A campaign can be paused or cancelled mid-flight.

Delivery is tracked per recipient

Queued, sent, delivered, read and failed are counted separately. WhatsApp fails individual messages constantly; a failed recipient is retried with backoff rather than the whole batch being re-sent because one number bounced.

Audiences

Build a segment from any of these rules:

Bought a specific productBought from a category
Lifetime spend betweenNumber of orders between
Has never bought anythingOrdered in the last N days
Has not ordered in the last N daysAbandoned a cart in the last N days
Delivery state is

Segment before you broadcast. "Bought once, more than 60 days ago" is a campaign. "Everyone" is how a list stops converting and starts generating blocks and reports.

Journeys — automated sequences

A journey runs when a customer does something, without you being involved. Enrolment happens on the event, not on a list upload.

Triggers

TriggerTypical use
New contact (welcome)Introduce the brand, set expectations
Cart abandonedA sequence rather than a single nudge
Browse abandoned (no cart)They looked but never added anything
Order placedReassure, set delivery expectations, cross-sell later
Order shippedTracking, then a review request after delivery

Steps

MessageSend on the channel you have configured
WaitHold for hours or days
FilterBranch, or drop out, based on what they have since done

The filter step is the one that matters most: it is what stops someone who has already bought receiving the rest of a "come back and buy" sequence.

Draft and live

Build a journey without it running, then switch it on. You can also enrol a specific customer by hand for testing.

Enrol yourself first and let the whole sequence run. Reading the steps in the editor is not the same as receiving them. Timing mistakes — three messages in an hour, or a review request before delivery — only become obvious on the receiving end.

Duplicate protection

A customer cannot be enrolled twice into the same active journey, so a repeat trigger does not produce two overlapping sequences.

Drafting copy, the shopping concierge, and connecting Claude.

Connecting a provider

Under Integrations → AI. You bring your own key, billed to your own account at cost: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (Groq, Together, DeepSeek, Mistral, OpenRouter, or a local Ollama).

Daily cost capA rupee limit checked before every call, so nothing can run up a bill overnight. Set one.
Cost per taskTokens in, tokens out and rupee cost are recorded on every generation.

Drafting content

AI can draft product copy, SEO meta, image alt text, FAQ blocks, and campaign and journey messages. It reads your existing published copy first, so drafts sound like your brand rather than like a model that has never seen your catalog.

Nothing is published without you. Every generation lands in a review queue. You apply it or reject it — applying is the only thing that touches live content.

What it can and cannot change

Generated text can only ever land in specific fields — name, description, SEO meta, alt text. It cannot touch a price, a stock level or an order status, however it is prompted.

Using it well

  • Give it good products to learn from. It copies the voice of what you have already written, so fix your best product page first.
  • Read every draft. It is a first draft, not a final one.
  • It is at its best on the boring bulk — alt text for 200 images, meta descriptions for a whole category.

The shopping concierge

With AI on, incoming WhatsApp and Instagram messages can be answered automatically — DMs and comment replies both.

  • It cannot invent a product, a price or a link. Your catalog is searched first and the model may only recommend from that shortlist. The product card in the reply is written by the store from the catalog row, not by the model.
  • It knows their last order — number and status — resolved only from a verified contact.
  • Every conversation lands in your inbox, so a person can take the thread at any point.
  • It degrades safely. With AI off or the provider having a bad day, it falls back to a fixed helpful reply rather than failing in front of a customer.

Watch the first fifty conversations. It answers from your catalog, so gaps in your product data show up as unhelpful answers. That is worth knowing early.

Connecting Claude or ChatGPT

Covered in full in Connecting Claude or ChatGPT. The short version:

Your store can be connected to Claude or ChatGPT directly, letting you ask questions in plain language — "which products are quietly running out of stock?", "what did last month's campaign actually earn?" — answered from your real data.

What it costs
The connector Nothing per query. It runs on the Claude or ChatGPT subscription you already pay for — no API key involved.
An API key Billed per token. Needed only for work that runs unattended: the concierge, and bulk generation.

Three tiers of access, and you decide where the line sits:

  • Draft — writes to the review queue and nowhere else. A human still applies it.
  • Write — changes live data. Off by default, behind a separate switch, and every change is audited.

Requirements, install, cron and going live, if you host it yourself.

This chapter is only for customers who chose to host the store themselves. If we host it for you, none of this applies — your store is already installed, updated and backed up.

You own the source code, so you can run it anywhere that meets the requirements below. Nothing phones home, and there is no licence check.

What your server needs

ComponentRequirementWhy
Operating systemUbuntu 22.04 or 24.04What the platform is built and tested against
Database MySQL 8 The schema uses utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci
PHP8.3 with FPM—
PHP extensions mysql, curl, mbstring, intl, xml, gd, imagick, zip, bcmath Images, invoices, imports, money maths
Web serverCaddy, or nginxCaddy issues HTTPS certificates by itself
CronAvailableQueued work, campaigns, cart recovery
Memory2 GB minimumImage processing is the hungry part
Disk20 GB and upProduct images grow faster than you expect

MariaDB will not work. It is a drop-in replacement for most things, but not for this schema's collation — migrations fail on the very first run. Many hosts advertise "MySQL" and provide MariaDB, so check before you pay: 

mysql -e "SELECT VERSION();"

If the answer contains MariaDB, that server cannot run the store.

Installing what you need

sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y mysql-server-8.0 \
  php8.3-fpm php8.3-mysql php8.3-curl php8.3-mbstring php8.3-intl \
  php8.3-xml php8.3-gd php8.3-imagick php8.3-zip php8.3-bcmath \
  imagemagick unzip cron

Then Caddy, which is not in Ubuntu's archive:

sudo apt install -y debian-keyring debian-archive-keyring apt-transport-https curl
curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/gpg.key' \
  | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/caddy-stable-archive-keyring.gpg
curl -1sLf 'https://dl.cloudsmith.io/public/caddy/stable/debian.deb.txt' \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-stable.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y caddy

Creating the database

sudo mysql
CREATE DATABASE gosell CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
CREATE USER 'gosell'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'a-long-random-password';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON gosell.* TO 'gosell'@'localhost';
FLUSH PRIVILEGES;
EXIT;

The collation on the first line is not optional — it is the one MariaDB lacks.

Putting the files in place

  1. Upload and extract the source we handed over, e.g. to /var/www/gosell.
  2. The web server's document root must be the public directory, not the project root.
sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/gosell
sudo chmod -R 755 /var/www/gosell
sudo chmod -R 775 /var/www/gosell/storage

Only public/ may be reachable from the web. If the document root is the project folder, your .env — database password included — is downloadable. This is the most damaging mistake on this page.

Configuration

Copy .env.example to .env and fill it in:

KeyWhat to put
APP_KEYA random 32-byte key, generated below. Never share it.
DB_HOST127.0.0.1 for a database on the same box
DB_PORT3306
DB_NAMEgosell
DB_USER / DB_PASSWORDWhat you created above
API_KEYA random string, if you use the API
FILE_SYSTEMlocal to start with
 
php -r "echo 'base64:' . base64_encode(random_bytes(32)) . PHP_EOL;"

Creating the tables

cd /var/www/gosell
php command migrate

If this fails on the first table, you are on MariaDB. If it fails on a missing extension, install it and run again — migrations are safe to re-run.

Web server

A minimal Caddyfile — Caddy obtains and renews HTTPS by itself:

yourstore.com {
    root * /var/www/gosell/public
    encode gzip
    php_fastcgi unix//run/php/php8.3-fpm.sock
    file_server
}
sudo systemctl reload caddy

Point your domain's A record at the server's IP first, or the certificate cannot be issued.

Cron — one line

* * * * * cd /var/www/gosell && php command schedule:run >> storage/logs/schedule.log 2>&1

That single entry runs everything on its own schedule: queued jobs, journeys, campaigns, cart scanning and session recovery.

Without cron, the store looks fine and silently does nothing in the background. No order emails, no cart recovery, no campaigns, no journeys — and no error to tell you. Add it during install, then confirm storage/logs/schedule.log is growing.

Creating your admin account

Nothing to run on the command line. Open https://yourstore.com/admin/ in a browser and you are taken straight to a one-time onboarding form — give it a name, a username and a password, and you are signed in.

That page closes itself permanently the moment the first account exists. From then on /admin/ is an ordinary login, and further staff are added from inside the admin. So there is no window where anyone can wander in and claim your store, as long as you do this step yourself rather than leaving a fresh install exposed overnight.

There is a command-line equivalent if you are scripting an install, or if you ever lock yourself out: 

php command make:admin yourname 'a-strong-password' 'Your Name'

Then finish setting up

From here it is the same as any store — work through First steps.

Before you take a real order

  • .env is not reachable over the web — try https://yourstore.com/.env and confirm you get an error, not a file.
  • HTTPS works and does not warn.
  • storage/logs/schedule.log is growing.
  • A test order completes and its confirmation email arrives.
  • A backup has run and you have restored it once somewhere else.

Keeping a self-hosted store safe and current.

Only for self-hosted stores. If we host yours, backups, patching and updates are ours to worry about.

Backups

Two things have to be backed up, and they are useless apart:

WhatContains
The databaseProducts, orders, customers, settings — everything you would cry about
storage/Product images and uploads
 
# Database
mysqldump -u gosell -p --single-transaction gosell \
  | gzip > /backups/gosell-$(date +%F).sql.gz

# Uploads
tar czf /backups/storage-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /var/www/gosell storage

Run both nightly from cron:

0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/gosell-backup.sh

A backup you have never restored is not a backup. Restore one onto a spare server, at least once, before you need to. Most backup scripts that "work" turn out to produce empty files, miss the uploads, or write to a disk that was full — and you find out on the worst possible day.

Keep a copy off the server

A backup on the same machine protects you from a mistake, not from losing the machine. Copy them somewhere else — object storage, another provider, anywhere that fails independently.

Restoring

gunzip < /backups/gosell-2026-08-26.sql.gz | mysql -u gosell -p gosell
tar xzf /backups/storage-2026-08-26.tar.gz -C /var/www/gosell

Then check file ownership, because a restore as root will have changed it:

sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/gosell/storage

Updating the platform

We publish releases and tell you what changed. Applying them is your call and your responsibility — nobody does it for you on a self-hosted store.

  1. Back up the database and storage/. Not optional.
  2. Read what changed.
  3. Put the new files in place, keeping your .env and storage/.
  4. Run php command migrate.
  5. Check the storefront and place a test order.

Do not update during your busiest hours, and never on a Friday evening. If something breaks you want to be awake, unhurried, and able to reach us.

Test somewhere else first, if you can

A copy of the store on a second server, updated first, turns a risky change into a boring one. Worth the extra machine once you are taking real money.

Keeping the server safe

  • Apply OS security updates. unattended-upgrades handles most of it.
  • Disable password SSH and use keys.
  • Firewall everything except 80, 443 and SSH. MySQL should not be reachable from the internet at all.
  • Do not reuse the database password anywhere else.
  • Check .env is not web-reachable after every change to the web server config.

What to watch

CheckHow oftenWhy
Disk spaceWeeklyImages and backups fill disks quietly; a full disk stops orders
storage/logs/schedule.log is growingWeeklyIf cron dies, background work stops with no error
Backups exist and are not emptyWeeklySilent failure is the normal failure
HTTPS certificate validIt renews itself — but checkAn expired certificate closes the shop
A test order completesMonthlyCatches an integration whose token quietly expired

We will help you deploy and hand over, and we would rather answer a question than have you guess. Day-to-day operation of your own server is yours — but ask anyway; we would rather you did.

  2. Category tiles or hand-picked products — something to click within a second.
  3. Trust badges — returns, delivery, secure payment.
  4. Image + text — the brand story, once they are interested.
  5. Reviews — other people vouching for you.
  6. FAQ — the objections that stop a first order.
  7. Newsletter — for the ones who are not ready today.

Resist adding every section. A home page with eleven sections is a page nobody reaches the bottom of. Cut anything that is not doing a job.

Beyond the home page, these are the ones customers look for and payment providers expect:

  • About — who is behind the shop. It converts better than people expect.
  • Contact — a real way to reach you.
  • Shipping policy — how long, how much, where you deliver.
  • Returns policy — the single most common reason a first order does not happen.
  • Privacy policy and Terms.

Menus are built separately under Navigation — creating a category or a page does not add it to a menu. That is deliberate: you often want something to exist and be linked from a campaign without cluttering the main menu.

Menu items can point at a category, a page, a feature (like the shop or search) or a custom URL. Menus nest, and you reorder them yourself.

Keep the main menu to about five items. Everything else belongs in the footer. A menu that needs two rows on a laptop is a menu nobody reads.

Meta, sitemaps, redirects and the SEO audit.

The unglamorous part that decides whether Google sends you anything. Most of it is done once and then left alone.

What happens without you

  • sitemap.xml is generated and regenerated as your catalog changes.
  • Clean URLs — readable slugs for products, categories and pages.
  • Automatic 301 redirects — rename a slug and the old URL redirects itself, so you keep the rankings you earned.
  • Structured markup — product data marked up for search engines.

The automatic redirect is worth understanding. Renaming a product slug on most platforms silently breaks every link to it. Here the old URL keeps working, so a link from a blog post two years ago still lands.

Meta titles and descriptions

Every product, category and page can override its title and description. Defaults are used where you leave them blank, which is fine for most of the catalog — spend the effort on the pages that matter.

FieldAim for
Meta titleUnder 60 characters, or Google truncates it
Meta descriptionUnder 155 characters. It does not affect ranking, but it decides whether anyone clicks.

The search-result preview shows how a title and description will actually appear before you save them.

The SEO audit

Measured coverage across your catalog: products missing a meta title, a description, body copy, images or alt text. A check that cannot be verified reports unknown rather than claiming a pass.

Work it in this order, because that is the order of impact:

  1. Products with no description at all.
  2. Products with no images, or images with no alt text.
  3. Missing meta titles on your best sellers.
  4. Everything else.

Alt text

Describe what is actually in the photograph, in plain words. It is read aloud to customers using a screen reader, shown when an image fails to load, and read by search engines. "Navy linen shirt on a wooden hanger" — not "IMG_4821" and not "buy shirt online india".

Internal links

The audit flags products and pages that nothing on your site links to. A page nothing links to is a page search engines struggle to find and customers never stumble across.

Being realistic

SEO is slow. Nothing here produces traffic this week. Do it because in six months you would rather have it done than be starting. If you need customers tomorrow, that is advertising, not SEO.

robots.txt

Editable under Settings. Leave it alone unless you know exactly why you are changing it — a stray Disallow: / removes your entire store from Google, and it takes weeks to come back.

Pointing a domain at your store and getting HTTPS.

Your store needs a domain of your own — usually yourbrand.com itself, though a subdomain like shop.yourbrand.com works just as well. Pointing it at the store takes one DNS record.

The DNS record

At your domain registrar — GoDaddy, Namecheap, BigRock, Cloudflare, wherever you bought the domain — add:

FieldValue
TypeA
NameYour full domain, e.g. yourbrand.com
ValueThe IP address you were given
TTLLeave the default

Some registrars want only the host part. For yourbrand.com itself that is @. For a subdomain such as shop.yourbrand.com it is shop. Both mean the same thing as entering the full name; use whichever your registrar expects.

HTTPS

Your certificate is issued automatically, usually within a minute of the domain resolving. You do not need to buy one, install one, or renew one — renewal is automatic too.

If you see a certificate warning immediately after changing DNS, wait a few minutes. It means the domain has only just started pointing here.

How long it takes

  • Most registrars apply the change within a few minutes.
  • Some take a few hours to propagate everywhere.
  • Until it propagates, some people may reach the store and others not. That is normal and resolves itself.

Checking it worked

dig +short yourbrand.com

That should print the IP you were given.

What you seeWhat it means
NothingNot saved, or still propagating. Wait an hour.
A different IPAn old A record, or a CNAME, is still in place
The right IPDone. The certificate follows within a minute or so.

Remove conflicting records. Delete any other A or AAAA record for the same name, and do not add a CNAME alongside. Two conflicting records is the most common reason a store appears down for some people and fine for others — which is far harder to diagnose than being down for everyone.

www or not

Pick one and be consistent. If you want both yourbrand.com and www.yourbrand.com to work, point both at the store; one will redirect to the other. Using both as separate addresses splits your SEO between them.

Tell the store its own address

Set Site URL under Settings → General to the address you settled on. Links in order emails and WhatsApp messages are built from it — get it wrong and every link you send points at the wrong place.
